subject_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: We are a body knit together by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope. We meet together as an assembly and a congregation. We pray together, we read scripture, we offer exhortation. Our presidents are elders, approved men. There is no buying and selling of any sort in the things of God. Even if there is a chest of sorts, it is not made up of purchase-money. On the monthly day, each puts in a small donation, if he will, and only if he be willing; for no one is compelled. These gifts are not spent on feasts or drinking bouts but to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined to the house.
passage.notes: Description of Christian assembly, common fund, and community life in Carthage

passage.excerpt: And so, according to the circumstances and disposition, and even age, of each individual, the delay of baptism is preferable; principally, however, in the case of little children. For why is it necessary — if baptism itself be not so necessary — that the sponsors likewise should be thrust into danger? Let them come, then, while they are growing up; let them come while they are learning, while they are being taught whither to come; let them become Christians when they have become able to know Christ.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: But to those who have stood firm and have not been overthrown, what great joy! Let them knock at the door of the Church, but not with violence to break it down; let them beg but not presumptuously demand. Proper penance under the bishop's authority must precede reconciliation.
